title: Rendering Models (CSR / SSR / SSG / ISR)
summary: Next.js can render a page in several ways — **client-side (CSR)**, **server-side per request (SSR)**, **statically at build time (SSG)**, or **statically with periodic regeneration (ISR)** — and choosing the right one per route is the core skill of using the framework well.

subtopics.title: Client-Side Rendering (CSR)
subtopics.explanation: The server sends a near-empty HTML shell plus JavaScript; the browser then fetches data and renders in the client. It's flexible and cheap to host, but the user sees a blank/loading state first and SEO suffers because crawlers may see little content. Good for private, highly interactive dashboards behind auth.

subtopics.title: Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
subtopics.explanation: Next renders the page to HTML on the server on every request, so the user gets fully-formed, data-filled HTML immediately and crawlers see real content. The trade-off is a slower TTFB (the server does work per request) and you need a running server. Use it for personalized or always-fresh pages.
subtopics.example:
// App Router: an async Server Component with no caching
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';

subtopics.title: Static Site Generation (SSG)
subtopics.explanation: Pages are rendered to HTML once at build time and served from a CDN, giving the fastest possible TTFB and great SEO. The catch is the content is frozen until the next build, so it's ideal for content that rarely changes — marketing pages, docs, blog posts.
subtopics.example:
// Default for a Server Component that fetches cacheable data
const posts = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json());

subtopics.title: Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)
subtopics.explanation: ISR is SSG plus a refresh interval: pages are served statically but regenerated in the background after a set time (or on demand), so you get static speed with eventually-fresh data. It's the sweet spot for content that changes occasionally, like a product catalog.
subtopics.example: fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 60 } }); // regenerate at most every 60s

subtopics.title: TTFB vs interactivity
subtopics.explanation: Server rendering (SSR/SSG/ISR) improves time-to-first-byte and first contentful paint because HTML arrives filled in, while CSR delays content until JS runs. But HTML still needs hydration to become interactive. The goal is to send meaningful HTML fast AND keep the JS needed for interactivity small.
subtopics.example: // SSG/ISR: instant HTML from CDN; CSR: blank until JS + fetch

subtopics.title: The build vs request boundary
subtopics.explanation: The key mental split: SSG/ISR do work at BUILD time (or in the background), while SSR does work on every REQUEST and CSR does work in the BROWSER. Where the work happens determines freshness, speed, cost, and whether you need a server.
subtopics.example: build time -> SSG/ISR | per request -> SSR | in browser -> CSR

foundations.overview: A page's rendering strategy decides where and when its HTML is produced. Next.js (App Router) lets you choose per route — and even mix strategies within a page using Server and Client Components. Picking correctly is what makes a Next.js app fast, fresh, and SEO-friendly without over-paying for server compute.
foundations.formalDefinition: Rendering strategy is the combination of where a route's HTML is generated (browser, server-per-request, or build time) and how its data is cached/revalidated. Next.js infers it from your data-fetching/caching choices and route config.
foundations.whyItMatters: The strategy directly controls SEO, perceived speed (TTFB/FCP), data freshness, and hosting cost. It's the single most-asked Next.js interview topic because it reveals whether you understand the framework's value proposition.
foundations.mentalModel: Ask two questions per route: (1) does the content change per user/often? and (2) does it need to be indexable/fast? CSR for private+interactive, SSR for fresh+personalized, SSG for stable+public, ISR for occasionally-changing+public.
foundations.browserPerspective: With server rendering the browser receives complete HTML it can paint immediately, then downloads JS to hydrate it into an interactive React tree. With CSR the browser paints almost nothing until JS loads and data arrives.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A marketing homepage is SSG, a logged-in dashboard is CSR (or SSR), a product page that updates a few times a day is ISR, and a personalized feed is SSR.
foundations.businessImpact: Faster first paint and proper SEO drive organic traffic and conversion; choosing SSG/ISR over SSR where possible also slashes server cost at scale.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Understanding the models prevents both extremes: needlessly server-rendering static content (wasting compute) and client-rendering content that needed SEO (losing traffic).
foundations.performanceImpact: SSG/ISR serve from a CDN (fastest, cheapest); SSR adds per-request latency and server load; CSR shifts work to the device and delays content. Right-sizing per route is the main perf lever.
commonUseCases: ISR for product catalogs and news that update periodically
SSR for personalized or always-fresh pages
CSR for private, highly interactive dashboards

commonMisconceptions.myth: SSR is always better than CSR.
commonMisconceptions.reality: SSR adds per-request server cost and latency. For private, highly interactive pages with no SEO need, CSR (or static shell + client data) is often the better choice.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You pick one rendering mode for the whole app.
commonMisconceptions.reality: In the App Router you choose per route, and even mix Server and Client Components within a single page.

steps.name: CSR
steps.detail: Server returns an empty shell + JS. The browser runs JS, fetches data, then renders. Slowest first paint, no SEO content, cheapest server.

steps.name: SSR
steps.detail: On each request the server fetches data and renders full HTML, then sends it. Fresh + SEO-friendly, but per-request cost and slower TTFB.

steps.name: SSG
steps.detail: At build time pages are pre-rendered to HTML and pushed to a CDN. Fastest TTFB and SEO, but content is frozen until the next build.

steps.name: ISR
steps.detail: Static like SSG, but after `revalidate` seconds the next request triggers a background rebuild. Static speed with periodic freshness.

steps.name: Hydration
steps.detail: For SSR/SSG/ISR the browser then loads JS and hydrates the HTML into an interactive React app.

codeLab.title: Decide the right strategy
codeLab.instructions: For each page, name the best rendering model and one reason. Edit the component to print your answers, then Run. (Marketing homepage; logged-in analytics dashboard; blog post updated weekly; personalized feed.)
codeLab.expectedOutput: Your reasoned choice for each page.
hints: Ask: does it need SEO/speed, and does it change per user/often?
Public + stable → SSG; public + occasional change → ISR; personalized/fresh → SSR; private + interactive → CSR.

debuggingLab.title: Why is my whole page client-rendered?
debuggingLab.symptom: A mostly-static marketing page ships a large JS bundle and loses SSG benefits.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Adding 'use client' to the top-level page makes the ENTIRE subtree a Client Component, so all that static content is client-rendered and shipped as JS — defeating SSG. Only the interactive bit needs to be a client component.
commonMistakes: Putting 'use client' at the top of a page just for one interactive widget.
Assuming Server Components can't contain Client Components (they can).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Keep the page a Server Component and extract ONLY the toggle into a small 'use client' child.

theory.question: What are the rendering strategies in Next.js and how do they differ?
theory.directAnswer: Next.js supports CSR (render in the browser), SSR (render HTML on the server per request), SSG (pre-render to static HTML at build time), and ISR (static with periodic background regeneration). They differ in WHERE and WHEN the HTML is produced, which drives SEO, speed, freshness, and cost — and in the App Router you choose per route via your data-fetching/caching options.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Four ways to produce a page's HTML: browser (CSR), server-per-request (SSR), build-time (SSG), or build-time-with-revalidation (ISR).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different pages have different needs for freshness, SEO, interactivity, and cost; one size doesn't fit all.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: In the App Router, a cacheable fetch → SSG, fetch with revalidate → ISR, no-store/dynamic → SSR, and a client component fetching in an effect → CSR.

theory.whyImportant: It's the defining Next.js skill and its most common interview question; getting it right is the difference between a fast, cheap, indexable app and a slow or expensive one.
theory.realWorldExample: Homepage = SSG, product page = ISR (revalidate hourly), account page = SSR, in-app dashboard = CSR.

nestedTopics.title: SSG vs ISR
nestedTopics.explanation: Both serve static HTML; ISR adds a revalidate window to refresh content without a full rebuild.

nestedTopics.title: SSR cost
nestedTopics.explanation: SSR renders per request, so it adds server latency and load vs CDN-served static pages.

nestedTopics.title: Per-route choice
nestedTopics.explanation: App Router decides the mode from each route's fetch/caching, not a global setting.

followUps.question: How do you turn a fetch into SSG vs ISR vs SSR?
followUps.answer: Default cache = SSG; fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: N } }) = ISR every N seconds; fetch(url, { cache: 'no-store' }) or export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' = SSR.

followUps.question: When is CSR still the right call?
followUps.answer: For private, highly interactive UIs behind auth where SEO doesn't matter and you want to minimize server work.

theory.question: What's the difference between SSG and ISR, and when would you choose ISR?
theory.directAnswer: SSG renders pages once at build time and they stay frozen until the next deploy; ISR serves those static pages but regenerates them in the background after a revalidate interval (or on demand). Choose ISR when content is public and benefits from static speed/SEO but changes too often to rebuild the whole site each time — like a product catalog or news section.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: ISR is SSG with a time-based (or on-demand) background refresh.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To get static performance for content that still needs to update without a full redeploy.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: After revalidate seconds, the next request serves the stale page and triggers a background regeneration; subsequent requests get the fresh page.

theory.whyImportant: ISR is the pragmatic default for large content sites and a frequent interview discriminator.
theory.realWorldExample: An e-commerce product page with revalidate: 3600 updates prices hourly without rebuilding thousands of pages on every change.

nestedTopics.title: On-demand revalidation
nestedTopics.explanation: revalidatePath/revalidateTag let you refresh specific pages when data changes, instead of waiting for the timer.

nestedTopics.title: Stale-while-revalidate
nestedTopics.explanation: Users get the cached page instantly while the new one builds in the background.

followUps.question: What does the first request after the revalidate window see?
followUps.answer: It still gets the cached (stale) page immediately and triggers regeneration; the fresh page is served to later requests.

scenario.question: A marketing site is slow to first paint and the team server-renders every page. How would you improve it?
scenario.directAnswer: Most marketing pages are public and stable, so I'd move them from SSR to SSG (or ISR if they change occasionally). That serves pre-built HTML from the CDN — far faster TTFB and much lower server cost — while keeping SEO. Only truly dynamic/personalized routes stay SSR.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A misapplied-SSR problem: static content rendered per request.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Teams sometimes default everything to dynamic rendering.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Making the data fetches cacheable (or adding revalidate) lets Next pre-render and serve statically.

scenario.whyImportant: Right-sizing rendering is the biggest perf/cost lever in Next.js.

nestedTopics.title: force-static / revalidate
nestedTopics.explanation: Opt routes into static or ISR rendering explicitly.

nestedTopics.title: Partial Prerendering
nestedTopics.explanation: Newer Next can serve a static shell while streaming dynamic holes.

followUps.question: How do you confirm a route is static vs dynamic?
followUps.answer: The build output marks each route (○ static, λ/ƒ dynamic), and you can inspect caching with the build summary and response headers.

coding.question: In the App Router, show how the same data fetch yields SSG, ISR, and SSR.
coding.thoughtProcess: Rendering mode follows the fetch's caching. A default fetch is cached → SSG. Adding next.revalidate makes it ISR. Setting cache: 'no-store' (or force-dynamic) makes it SSR. I'll show all three in a Server Component.
coding.lineByLine: The default fetch is cached, so the page is statically generated. next.revalidate: 60 keeps it static but refreshes in the background every 60s (ISR). cache: 'no-store' opts out of caching, forcing per-request server rendering (SSR).
coding.timeComplexity: N/A — rendering strategy, not an algorithm.

alternativeApproaches.title: Route segment config
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Set the mode for a whole route instead of per fetch.
alternativeApproaches.code: export const revalidate = 60; // or: export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';

followUps.question: If one fetch on the page is no-store, what happens to the page?
followUps.answer: Any uncached/dynamic data opts the route into dynamic (SSR) rendering for that request.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Treat rendering as a per-route decision in the App Router: static shell where possible, server-render the dynamic parts, and push personalization to Client Components or streamed segments. Partial Prerendering blends a static shell with streamed dynamic holes.
productionDeepDive.performance: Prefer SSG/ISR (CDN-served) for anything cacheable; reserve SSR for truly dynamic routes. Keep Client Components small to minimize hydration JS. Use revalidateTag/Path for targeted freshness instead of global no-store.
productionDeepDive.security: Server rendering keeps secrets and data access on the server; never leak tokens into Client Components. Validate and authorize inside server code/route handlers, not the client.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Static/ISR pages scale via CDN almost for free; SSR scales with server capacity, so isolate expensive SSR routes and cache aggressively. On-demand revalidation avoids rebuild storms.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Make each route's strategy explicit (route config) so reviewers can see why a page is dynamic; document why any route opts out of caching.
productionDeepDive.observability: The build output labels each route static/dynamic; monitor TTFB, cache HIT/MISS, and revalidation behavior in production (e.g., Vercel analytics/logs).

caseStudies.problem: Thousands of pages that change occasionally but must be fast and indexable.
caseStudies.solution: ISR with on-demand revalidation so pages are static yet refresh when data changes.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Eventual consistency (a revalidate window) vs full freshness.
caseStudies.lessons: ISR is the default for big content sites; reserve SSR for genuinely per-request data.

keyTakeaways: Next.js renders per route as CSR, SSR, SSG, or ISR — chosen by your data-fetching/caching, not a global flag.
SSG/ISR serve static HTML from a CDN (fastest, cheapest); SSR renders per request (fresh but costly); CSR renders in the browser (interactive, no SEO).
ISR = SSG + background revalidation: static speed with periodic freshness, ideal for large content sites.
Keep Client Components small — only the interactive parts need 'use client' — to preserve static benefits and reduce hydration JS.
Pick a strategy by asking: does it need SEO/speed, and does it change per user or often?
